# Week 37, 2026

Highlights selected from everything kept between September 4, 2026 and September 11, 2026. Items are selected several times a day by an automated pipeline and the summaries are machine generated; follow the links to the original sources. See [About](../../about.md) for how selection works.

## The week in brief

<div class="section-brief">
<p>A randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Indonesia, Kenya, and the Netherlands found that physicians with access to GPT-4o, a large language model (LLM), outperformed those without it, with the largest gain, 18 percentage points, in the Kenyan sample <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03111-5">[2]</a>. The caveats matter as much as the effect: controls had no internet or guideline access, harms were not assessed, and the authors note the results come from controlled conditions rather than real practice <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03111-5">[2]</a>. A Nature Medicine commentary on one of the first RCTs of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine argues that tools should be judged on whether human-AI systems improve patient outcomes, not on whether algorithms match clinicians <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04633-x">[1]</a>. A call for collaborators on the Validation Accords adds that real-world validation of generative AI is often omitted <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04647-5">[5]</a>.</p>
<p>Deployment reports point to the same gap. Implementers of an AI-agent eye clinic in China report that AI-native care requires workflow integration, clinician engagement, and measurable clinical value <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04631-z">[6]</a>. ARPA-H, the government agency funding health research, committed $62.7 million toward partially autonomous AI for heart failure, authorized by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), to assess symptoms, prescribe drugs, and order lab tests for patients without specialist access <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/09/09/arpa-h-advocate-program-autonomous-ai-bots-for-heart-failure">[7]</a>.</p>
<p>An international working group&#x27;s framework of seven domains and 24 learning objectives holds that AI education must be clinically grounded, ethically integrated, and implementation-aware <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03197-x">[8]</a>. The three-country trial is a ready case: students can name what its controls lacked and why unassessed harms limit the conclusion <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03111-5">[2]</a>.</p>
<p class="section-brief-date">Written from the items highlighted below; numbered links go to the sources.</p>
</div>
